decisions.mark: locates the macro's definition in include/mbedtls/private_access.h
decisions.detail: QUOTE: "`MBEDTLS_PRIVATE(member)` is a token-paste macro, defined in `include/mbedtls/private_access.h:14-18`" | WHY: The answer explicitly states the macro's definition location in include/mbedtls/private_access.h and quotes the definition.

decisions.mark: states that by default the macro RENAMES the member to private_<member>, and that defining MBEDTLS_ALLOW_PRIVATE_ACCESS makes it expand to the member name unchanged
decisions.detail: QUOTE: `#define MBEDTLS_PRIVATE(member) private_##member` ... `#else #define MBEDTLS_PRIVATE(member) member` (under `#ifndef MBEDTLS_ALLOW_PRIVATE_ACCESS`) | WHY: The answer shows the macro expanding to private_##member by default and to the plain member when MBEDTLS_ALLOW_PRIVATE_ACCESS is defined, and explains this in prose.

decisions.mark: explains that the two branches give different consumers different views — code that defines MBEDTLS_ALLOW_PRIVATE_ACCESS sees plain member names while an ordinary consumer of the public headers sees the renamed ones
decisions.detail: QUOTE: Only translation units that define `MBEDTLS_ALLOW_PRIVATE_ACCESS` before the first include of `private_access.h` see the real names. ... The default is the external user. ... Public headers declare struct members as `MBEDTLS_PRIVATE(state)`, so the member is really named `private_state`. A user writing `ssl->state` gets a compile error. | WHY: The answer states that code defining the opt-out macro sees the real plain names, while ordinary external consumers see the `private_`-prefixed names.

decisions.mark: concludes that this enforces API opacity at COMPILE time by breaking the member name, rather than by hiding the struct layout — the fields remain visible and sized
decisions.detail: QUOTE: "This is name-mangling, not access control: C has no access control, and the layout is identical either way. What it buys is that accidental use fails at compile time" | WHY: The answer says the macro renames members (`private_state`) so access fails at compile time, while the layout stays unchanged, which matches the item.

decisions.mark: conveys that the macro is applied at a scale of many hundreds of sites, overwhelmingly in the public headers rather than in library implementation
decisions.detail: QUOTE: NONE | WHY: The answer never says the macro is applied at many hundreds of sites or that usage is overwhelmingly in public headers rather than library implementation.

decisions.mark: states that library-internal code turns the opt-out ON in a shared header, so every library translation unit sees plain member names
decisions.detail: QUOTE: `library/common.h:132` | Defines the opt-out unconditionally. Library `.c` files that include `common.h` first (for example `library/ssl_tls.c:12`, ...) read and write struct members by their plain names. | WHY: The answer states that the shared header common.h defines MBEDTLS_ALLOW_PRIVATE_ACCESS, so library translation units see plain member names.

decisions.mark: identifies that some example programs ALSO define the opt-out for themselves, deliberately reaching past the public API they otherwise demonstrate
decisions.detail: QUOTE: `programs/ssl/ssl_server2.c:8` | Defined before `ssl_test_lib.h`, so the in-tree test server reaches into SSL internals directly. | `programs/ssl/ssl_client2.c:8` | Same, for the client. | WHY: The answer states that the example programs ssl_server2.c and ssl_client2.c define MBEDTLS_ALLOW_PRIVATE_ACCESS themselves and reach into SSL internals directly.
